intro: A second, much larger round. The detector ran on 7,661 unseen images from three public sources (everyday photos, web photos across 105 animal species, and forest camera traps by day and by night). The touch classifier ran on 6,231 crops split into 8 kinds of example, plus 103 hands at real plants taken from Open Images and labelled by eye, under 17 kinds of camera damage. Every clip was replayed as 7 worse cameras would record it. Slice galleries are seeded random samples, so they show typical behaviour rather than the best cases.
det_overview: Our detector is the only one of the four that works on forest camera traps: mAP50 0.785, against 0.32 and 0.38 for the stock yolo26n and yolo26s, which find under a quarter of the animals there. This is what the fine-tuning bought. On everyday COCO photos the stock yolo26s is ahead (0.751 against 0.664); on Open Images ours leads (0.781 against 0.723); over all 7,661 images ours and yolo26s are level (0.703 against 0.695). The deployed ONNX file stays within 0.015 of the PyTorch weights on every set. The fold spread (about ±0.01 to 0.03) is far smaller than the gaps between image sets, so the kind of scene matters much more than which images happen to be drawn.
det_slices: Object size is the strongest factor: 84% of large objects are found, 63% of medium ones and 28% of small ones (18% of small plants). Crowded scenes with 5 or more objects drop to 59%, against 84% for a single object. Darkness barely matters: on the camera traps 70% of animals are found by day and 69% in night infrared, and dark colour photos sit at 68% against 70% for normal ones. Objects cut by the frame edge are found more often (77%), because they are usually big close-ups. At the bottom of the species list, Open Images' generic 'Mammal' and 'Animal' labels are mostly boxes on people (159 of the 372 'Mammal' boxes were found, but called person). The real misses are camouflaged forest animals on leaf litter: partridges, murids, squirrels and the spotted linsang, found 32 to 46% of the time.
det_errors: Looking at the false boxes one by one, many are not mistakes. The most confident 'background' boxes include a llama, a cat on a bed and a bush next to a fire hydrant: real animals and plants the dataset never labelled (COCO has no llama class and labels only potted plants). Others are genuine: a bronze statue as a person, a painted cow sculpture and a jet of muddy water as animals, a vase of peacock feathers as a plant. Most 'wrong class' boxes come from Open Images labelling people as 'Mammal', so our model's person box counts as wrong. The real class errors are rare and odd: a close-up face and a skateboarder called animal. The largest misses are mostly label artefacts too: roast turkeys labelled as the animal Turkey, a cartoon-pig costume, and camera-trap frames where an animal fills the whole lens as a blur. Poor boxes (722) are as common as background boxes (714). In the gallery they are a mix: one box round two animals that touch (porcupines, chickens, elephants), a whole snake boxed where the label marks only its head, and animals seen through bicycle spokes.
touch_kinds: The classifier is excellent at staying quiet: 99.4% of hands near a plant but not touching it are left alone, and 84 to 89% of free hands and hands on the body. Where it struggles is contact without a grip. Hands holding an object are caught 71% of the time, but a hand resting flat on a fixed object (a table, a wall, a tree) only 51%. The random gallery shows why: flat palms on tables score 0.06 to 0.2, while fingers curled round something score 0.8 to 1.0. Hands on a plant from the test splits are caught in only 1 of 10 crops. Ten crops is too few to judge, so a second, external set was built below. Blurry crops (74.5% right against 80.2% for sharp ones) and crops full of green leaves (68.8%, only 80 crops) are also harder.
touch_oi: The same pattern, now on 103 independent crops. Hands that grip something, such as a flower stem, a bouquet or a bundle of stalks, are caught with scores of 0.74 to 0.97. A flat hand on grass, a palm on tree bark, or fingers brushing through wheat score 0.00 to 0.40 and are missed. At the app's 0.6 threshold it caught 6 of 31 touches with 1 false touch in 72. Lowering the threshold to 0.3 catches 15 of 31. The scores still put touches above non-touches, so the model is ranking sensibly but is too cautious for plant contact. This is why the app's leaf-movement rule matters, and it is the clearest case for retraining with crops of hands on plants.
touch_damage: Overexposure, fog and mirroring cost under 2 points even at full strength, and the canopy-green tint, low contrast and an off-centre crop (the pose model placing the hand a little wrong) cost about 3. Blur, rotation and a zoomed-out crop (the pose model sizing the hand too big) cost 6 to 10 points, and leaves covering a third of the crop 12. The damaging ones are the grainy kinds: sensor noise (0.534 at strength 3), pixelation from distance (0.561), dusk light with noise (0.595), heavy JPEG (0.606) and rain (0.648). All of them hit fine texture, and the strip pictures show the score falling as grain appears. Training with noise, JPEG and low-light augmentation is the obvious fix. Mirror test-time augmentation (averaging each crop with its mirror image) adds about half a point of accuracy (0.790 against 0.785) for twice the work.
cond: Fog, sensor noise, dusk and a 640-pixel camera made no difference to any clip: every expected alert still came, and 'look plants' stayed alert-free. Heavy JPEG cost one clip (touch plants 2: the score peaked at 0.85 but never held for the 4 frames an ALERT needs). Night infrared is the real weakness and cost three clips. On 'touch plants 2' (a bare forearm reaching into a bush) the person detector found nobody in any greyscale frame, against every frame in colour. On 'ivy_touch' pose found a hand in only 18 of 168 frames, against 157 in colour. On 'video2_4k' hands were still found, but the touch score reached 0.6 in only 9 frames, against 259 in colour. This matches the greyscale drop in the touch tests: a night camera would need a model trained on infrared frames.
